title: The Asylum, the Prison, the Bathhouse: Foucault and the Institutions That Look Back
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Poitiers, birth in the surgeon's house
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the house on rue Arthur-Ranc a son is born to Paul Foucault, surgeon and son of a surgeon, and to Anne Malapert, herself a surgeon's daughter. The father enters the boy in the register as Paul-Michel, keeping the family name attached to the family trade. The mother calls him Michel, and Michel is the name he answers to for the rest of his life. The town is provincial, Catholic, built of pale stone, and the professions in it are inherited. He will spend forty years writing the history of clinics and asylums, and never practice medicine for a day.
suggested_refs: The Foucault family house at 10 rue Arthur-Ranc, Poitiers

stops.name: Poitiers, the lycee entered two years early
stops.date_confidence: the chronology lens gives the year 1930 with no month or day; day and month here are placeholders
stops.campa: He is put into the Lycee Henri-IV of Poitiers two years ahead of his age, small among older boys, because his mother will not have him left behind. His marks are strong and never brilliant. The teachers report a child who reads faster than he is taught and who does not much like the company of the classroom. The war arrives in the middle of this schooling and the school does not survive it intact. His father wants a surgeon out of him, a third in the line. He is already refusing.
suggested_refs: The Lycee Henri-IV of Poitiers, now Lycee Camille-Guerin

stops.name: Poitiers, College Saint-Stanislas under the occupation
stops.date_confidence: contested year: the chronology lens says 1939, the geography lens 1940-1943, and the German occupation of France begins only in June 1940; 1940 is adopted here and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved
stops.campa: Threatened with repeating a year, he is moved by his parents to the Catholic College Saint-Stanislas, where the Jesuit discipline suits him exactly. His marks rise sharply. He takes first places in history, philosophy and Greek, and in 1943 the baccalaureat in philosophy. Outside the classroom the town is occupied, the Kommandantur sits a few streets away, and a schoolmate disappears into the maquis. What he remembers of the period afterwards is the menace: a public order nobody voted for reaching into the private life of families.
suggested_refs: College Saint-Stanislas, Poitiers, wartime registers
sources: David Macey, The Lives of Michel Foucault

stops.name: Paris, Lycee Henri-IV and the class of Jean Hyppolite
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1945 by the chronology lens; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: He is sent to Paris to board in the rue Clovis and prepare the entrance examination for the Ecole Normale Superieure. Jean Hyppolite, who has put Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit into French, takes the class in history and philosophy. Foucault hears the Phenomenology explained sentence by sentence by the man who rebuilt it in his own language, and decides that philosophy is a thing done with texts rather than with opinions. Twenty-five years later the chair he is elected to at the College de France is the one Hyppolite held.
suggested_refs: Lycee Henri-IV, 23 rue Clovis, Paris 5e, the khagne of 1945-1946

stops.name: Paris, the Ecole Normale Superieure at 45 rue d'Ulm
stops.date_confidence: attested for the September 1946 entrance, ranked fourth; the geography lens adds that this was his second attempt, which the chronology lens does not mention, and the two are left standing side by side
stops.campa: He enters the rue d'Ulm at the second attempt, ranked fourth of his year, and is at once disliked: a sarcastic provincial who works alone at night and quarrels by daylight. In 1948 he takes his degree in philosophy. In the same years the depression closes over him and he attempts his own life; the school doctor files the misery under a homosexuality that no one at the rue d'Ulm will name aloud. Louis Althusser, the young caiman of the school, protects him.
suggested_refs: The Ecole Normale Superieure, 45 rue d'Ulm, class of 1946
sources: Macey, The Lives of Michel Foucault

stops.name: Paris, the Sorbonne, a licence in psychology
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1949 by the chronology lens; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: Alongside the diplome d'etudes superieures in philosophy he takes a licence in psychology at the Sorbonne, an unusual double load that puts him in the laboratory and the lecture hall at once. He is reading Binswanger, Jaspers, the Gestalt psychologists, Pavlov in translation. The licence is finished in 1949, three years before he first walks the wards at Sainte-Anne. In these same amphitheatres, sixteen years earlier, Antonin Artaud had stood before an audience and acted out the plague until people walked out laughing.
suggested_refs: The Sorbonne, licence de psychologie, 1949

stops.name: Paris, the agregation failed, the Party joined
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1950 for the failure and the Party membership, 1951 for the pass; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: He fails the agregation at the first attempt, in front of a jury that finds him arrogant, and the failure knocks him flat. The same year he joins the French Communist Party, brought in by Althusser and never comfortable there. In 1951 he passes at the second attempt and takes a research post at the Fondation Thiers, which he abandons within a year. The doctoral thesis he begins in this period is dropped. In the same period he is teaching psychology at the Ecole Normale, to students a year or two behind him.
suggested_refs: The Fondation Thiers, Paris, research fellowship 1951-1952

stops.name: Paris, Hopital Sainte-Anne, the intern with no title
stops.date_confidence: the geography lens dates the Sainte-Anne period 1952-1955; month and day are placeholders. The interlock lens carries a different Sainte-Anne pin, 48.8236 / 2.3277, from the Barthes file; the disagreement is recorded in the report
stops.campa: He takes a Specialist Diploma in Psychopathology and spends three years in the wards of Sainte-Anne with no defined status at all: not a doctor, not a patient, not quite a student, walking the corridors in a white coat nobody has authorized. He attends the clinical presentations, where a professor exhibits a madman to a room of students and questions him in front of them. In these same wards, in 1938, Jacques Lacan had pronounced on the incurability of Antonin Artaud.
suggested_refs: Hopital Sainte-Anne, 1 rue Cabanis, Paris 14e, the clinical presentations

stops.name: Lille, the psychology lectures and an August in Italy
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1953 by the chronology lens; month and day are placeholders, and the coordinate is a city-centre geocode because the pool records no campus location
stops.campa: He teaches psychology at the University of Lille, commuting north with his lecture notes and his Sainte-Anne files. In August, on holiday in Italy, he reads Nietzsche's Untimely Meditations in the sun and afterwards says that everything began there: the sense that a concept has a history, and that the history is a fight. Nietzsche had corrected the proofs of the Genealogy of Morals at Venice in 1887. In 1954 Foucault publishes his first book, Maladie mentale et personnalite, and a long introduction to Binswanger's Dream and Existence.
suggested_refs: Maladie mentale et personnalite (PUF, 1954); the Binswanger introduction

stops.name: Uppsala, the Maison de France and the medical library
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1955 by both lenses for the arrival; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: He leaves France for five years of cultural diplomacy, first as reader in French language and literature at Uppsala and director of the Maison de France. He lectures on French letters to Swedish students who arrive in the dark and leave in the dark, and works nights in the university library, whose medical holdings run to thousands of volumes on illness, quarantine and confinement from the fifteenth century onward. The book he begins out of that collection will be a thesis of nearly a thousand pages on madness.
suggested_refs: The Carolina Rediviva library at Uppsala and its Waller medical collection
sources: Macey, The Lives of Michel Foucault

stops.name: Warsaw, the Centre francais and the trap
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1958 by the chronology lens; the geography lens gives the Warsaw period as 1958-1959
stops.campa: He is posted to Warsaw as cultural attache and director of the Centre francais at the university. Poland is two years past the thaw of October 1956 and the security services still work by leverage. A young man is put in his way by the security services; the affair is photographed; the embassy is informed and the ministry recalls him. He leaves the country abruptly, his diplomatic career finished in under a year. Sources agree on the entrapment and disagree on its details.
suggested_refs: The Centre de civilisation francaise, University of Warsaw, 1958-1959

stops.name: Hamburg, the Institut francais and the finished thesis
stops.date_confidence: contested year: the chronology lens puts the Hamburg post in 1958, the geography lens in 1959-1960, and French sources give the directorship as 1 October 1959 to 30 September 1960; 1959 is adopted here and the contradiction is recorded
stops.campa: The last of the diplomatic posts sends him to the Institut francais in Hamburg, where he directs a language school by day and finishes Folie et deraison by night, alone, in a city he barely enters. The manuscript, nearly a thousand pages of it, is complete by 1960. He has written a history of the reason of Europe from outside Europe's centre, in Sweden, Poland and Germany, using foreign libraries, and he comes home with it under his arm to a country that has no post for him.
suggested_refs: The Institut francais de Hambourg, directorship 1959-1960

stops.name: Clermont-Ferrand, the tenured post and the commute
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1960 by the chronology lens; the geography lens gives the Clermont years as 1960-1966. The meeting with Daniel Defert is dated by the pool only as 'c. 1960s' and its placement in this stop is a reconstruction
stops.campa: He takes a philosophy post at Clermont-Ferrand and refuses to live there, commuting down from Paris and teaching in concentrated blocks. In 1962 he takes over the position of Jules Vuillemin. A student named Daniel Defert comes into his orbit; the relationship that begins in these years runs until his death, non-monogamous and never hidden between them. In 1966 he tries to have Gilles Deleuze appointed to the faculty and is overruled by a university that does not want either of them.
suggested_refs: The Faculte des lettres of Clermont-Ferrand, 1960-1966

stops.name: Paris, the Sorbonne, the soutenance of the thesis
stops.date_confidence: attested to 20 May 1961
stops.campa: He defends Folie et deraison at the Sorbonne before a jury presided over by Henri Gouhier, with Georges Canguilhem as rapporteur, the historian of the life sciences who read the manuscript and backed it. The secondary thesis is a translation of Immanuel Kant's Anthropology from a Pragmatic Point of View with a commentary on it. Plon publishes the book that month. It sells slowly and is reviewed by Blanchot and Barthes. An abridged English translation follows in 1964.
stops.quote: One day, perhaps, we will no longer know what madness was.
stops.quote_source: 'Madness, the absence of an oeuvre' (1964), Appendix I to History of Madness, trans. Jonathan Murphy and Jean Khalfa (Routledge, 2006), foucault.info excerpt
suggested_refs: Folie et deraison: Histoire de la folie a l'age classique (Plon, 1961); the Kant Anthropology thesis

stops.name: Paris, Naissance de la clinique
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1963 by the chronology lens; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: In one year he publishes two books: Naissance de la clinique, on how the doctor's eye learned to read the body as a text of lesions, and Raymond Roussel, on a writer who built machines out of sentences and died of barbiturates in Palermo. The clinic book dates the birth of the medical gaze to the moment when the question put to the sick stops being what is the matter with you and becomes where does it hurt. It is the same Paris medicine that Sigmund Freud came to study under Charcot at the Salpetriere in the winter of 1885.
suggested_refs: Naissance de la clinique (PUF, 1963); Raymond Roussel (Gallimard, 1963)

stops.name: Paris, Les Mots et les choses sells like hot cakes
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1966 by the chronology lens; the day is a placeholder
stops.campa: The Order of Things appears in April. It sells out, is reprinted, is argued about in the weekly magazines, and makes its author a public name. The press files him with Claude Levi-Strauss, Lacan and Barthes under the label structuralism, which he rejects in every interview he gives. That October, at the Johns Hopkins colloquium in Baltimore where Barthes, Lacan and Derrida convene to introduce the new French thought to America, Foucault does not come.
suggested_refs: Les Mots et les choses (Gallimard, 1966); the 1966 Johns Hopkins colloquium

stops.name: Tunis, the chair at the university
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1966 by the chronology lens; the day is a placeholder
stops.campa: He takes a teaching post at the University of Tunis in September 1966, at the height of his Paris fame, and leaves the fame behind. He lectures on Descartes, on Nietzsche, on painting, to students who arrive at his classes from political meetings. Defert is doing his national service in Tunisia, and that is half the reason for the move; the light and the distance from Paris are the other half. He stays two years. It is the first post he has taken outside Europe.
suggested_refs: The Faculty of Letters, University of Tunis, 1966-1968

stops.name: Sidi Bou Said, the villa above the sea
stops.date_confidence: the geography lens dates the residence 1966-1968; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: He rents a house in the white and blue village on the cliff north of Tunis and writes L'Archeologie du savoir there, the book in which he sets out the rules of his own method after the fact. In June 1967 anti-government riots break out in the capital and he is in the middle of them. Students come to the villa afterwards; he hides their papers and lets them work in his rooms. The archaeology of knowledge is drafted in a house that is also a depot.
suggested_refs: The villa at Sidi Bou Said where L'Archeologie du savoir was drafted
sources: Macey, The Lives of Michel Foucault

stops.name: Tunis, the crackdown on the students
stops.date_confidence: contested date: the geography lens places the repression that shook him in June 1968, the chronology lens attests anti-government riots in June 1967, and the March 1968 student movement is the crackdown the biographies describe; March 1968 is adopted and the disagreement is recorded
stops.campa: The Tunisian student movement is broken by police. Young men from his lecture room are beaten, tried and given sentences of eight and ten and fourteen years. Foucault hides a duplicating machine in his garden, testifies where he can, and is roughed up himself. He is not in Paris that May. He says afterwards that what he saw in Tunis was more serious than what happened in France, because in Tunis the students risked everything they had, and that it was the Tunisian experience, not the French one, that turned him into a militant.
suggested_refs: The March 1968 student movement at the University of Tunis and its trials
sources: Macey, The Lives of Michel Foucault

stops.name: Vincennes, the philosophy department of Paris VIII
stops.date_confidence: the chronology lens gives only 1968; the experimental centre at Vincennes opens its philosophy department in December 1968 and teaches from January 1969, so the month here is a reconstruction
stops.campa: He comes back from Tunis into a France still smoking from May and is handed the philosophy department of the new experimental university in the woods at Vincennes. He staffs it with the militant left, brings Gilles Deleuze in at last, and lets the students hold the building. The ministry withdraws recognition of the department's degrees within two years. In 1969 he publishes L'Archeologie du savoir, drafted above the sea at Sidi Bou Said, and begins the campaign for a chair at the College de France.
suggested_refs: The Centre universitaire experimental de Vincennes, philosophy department, 1968-1970

stops.name: Paris, the College de France, the election
stops.date_confidence: the chronology lens dates the election to November 1969; the College de France's own chair records state that the chair Histoire des systemes de pensee was created in November 1969 and that Foucault was elected on 12 April 1970 by 24 votes of 39 cast. The College's date is adopted and the conflation is recorded
stops.campa: The assembly of professors creates a chair in the history of systems of thought, the chair that replaces Jean Hyppolite's, and elects Foucault to it by twenty-four votes of thirty-nine. He is forty-three. The College has no students, no examinations and no degrees: a professor is required only to give a public course each year on work in progress, to anyone who walks in off the street. He will hold the chair for fourteen years and never write a book that is not connected to those winter lectures.
suggested_refs: College de France, chaire Histoire des systemes de pensee, election of 12 April 1970

stops.name: Paris, the inaugural lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1970 by the chronology lens; the day is a placeholder, and the lecture is generally dated 2 December 1970
stops.campa: He gives the inaugural lecture, L'Ordre du discours, to an overfull amphitheatre on the Place Marcelin-Berthelot: an argument that every society controls what may be said by procedures of exclusion, prohibition and division, beginning with the division between reason and madness. He opens by saying he would have preferred to be enveloped in speech and carried beyond all possible beginnings. That autumn he has also been teaching as a visiting professor in the French department at Buffalo, in the state of New York.
suggested_refs: L'Ordre du discours, inaugural lecture at the College de France, December 1970

stops.name: Paris, the Groupe d'Information sur les Prisons is declared
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1971 by the chronology lens; the day is a placeholder
stops.campa: With Pierre Vidal-Naquet and Jean-Marie Domenach he founds the Groupe d'Information sur les Prisons and gives its address as his own flat. The group refuses to speak for prisoners; it prints questionnaires, smuggles them in through families, and publishes the answers unedited. Defert runs much of it. That March a twenty-one-year-old Argentine named Luis Alberto Spinetta walks this city still ringing with May 68, reading Rimbaud in French and drinking from Foucault and from Artaud's madness, and carries the reading home to Buenos Aires.
suggested_refs: GIP, Intolerable pamphlets 1-4 (1971-1973)

stops.name: Paris, the gates of La Sante
stops.date_confidence: the geography lens dates the GIP actions at La Sante to 1971-1972 without exact days; May 1971 is a placement inside that span, not an attested date
stops.campa: The group works the pavement outside the walls of La Sante, in the fourteenth arrondissement, stopping wives and mothers on visiting days and asking them what the inside is like: the food, the cells, the punishments, the mail. Foucault stands there with a leaflet in his hand and is moved on by the police for it. He is by now a professor at the College de France. The distance between the amphitheatre on the Place Marcelin-Berthelot and this gate is two kilometres, and he crosses it every week.
suggested_refs: The prison de la Sante, rue de la Sante, Paris 14e

stops.name: Paris, the Goutte d'Or and Djellali Ben Ali
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1971 by the chronology lens; the day is a placeholder
stops.campa: A fifteen-year-old Algerian boy, Djellali Ben Ali, is shot dead by a building caretaker in the Goutte d'Or. Foucault takes to the street over it, with Genet and Claude Mauriac and Jean-Paul Sartre, forming a committee of inquiry into the killing and into what the newspapers do not call racism. He speaks through a megaphone in a quarter where nobody has read a word of him. The committee meets in the Goutte d'Or itself and goes on meeting there through the winter of 1971.
suggested_refs: The Comite Djellali, Goutte d'Or, Paris 18e, winter 1971

stops.name: Toul, the revolt in the central prison
stops.date_confidence: the geography lens dates the GIP's Toul work to 1971-1972; the revolt at the maison centrale breaks out in December 1971
stops.campa: The prisoners of the maison centrale at Toul take the roof. The prison psychiatrist, Edith Rose, breaks her silence and publishes what she has seen inside: the chains, the isolation cells, the punishments that are not in any regulation. The GIP amplifies her report until the ministry cannot ignore it and a director is removed. Foucault goes to Toul, reads the documents, keeps the file. Four years later the file has become a book about how the modern penalty came to consist of time measured out inside walls.
suggested_refs: Dr Edith Rose's report on the Toul central prison, December 1971

stops.name: Attica, the prison seven months after the massacre
stops.date_confidence: the geography lens dates the visit to April 1972; the day is a placeholder
stops.campa: He is taken through Attica Correctional Facility in western New York, seven months after the uprising in which the state's own troopers killed twenty-nine prisoners and ten hostages retaking the yard. He describes it afterwards to the interviewer John K. Simon as an immense machine, a factory whose product is the elimination of people it has first manufactured as criminals. He knows this landscape a little: he taught at Buffalo, forty miles west, in 1970.
suggested_refs: 'Michel Foucault on Attica: an interview' with John K. Simon (1972)
sources: Macey, The Lives of Michel Foucault
Foucault, radio and print interview transcripts, 1972

stops.name: Paris, arrested beside Jean Genet
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1972 by the chronology lens; the day is a placeholder
stops.campa: An Algerian worker, Mohammad Diab, is shot dead in a police station at Versailles. At the demonstration that follows, Foucault is arrested along with Jean Genet and thrown into a van; Genet takes a beating in the cells and Foucault writes it up. The following year he helps found the Agence de Presse-Liberation and then the newspaper Liberation itself, on the principle that people should be able to report their own lives rather than have them reported.
suggested_refs: Agence de Presse-Liberation and the founding of Liberation, 1973

stops.name: Paris, Surveiller et punir
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1975 by the chronology lens; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: The book opens with the public torture of the regicide Damiens in 1757 and closes in a prison that no longer touches the body at all, and it argues that the second is not progress but a change of technique. At its centre is Bentham's Panopticon, the ring of cells around a tower from which one guard may be watching and nobody can tell. Four years of leaflets at the gates of La Sante and the file from Toul are inside it. The prisons, he writes, resemble factories, schools, barracks and hospitals, which all resemble prisons.
stops.quote_source: Discipline and Punish (1977), trans. Alan Sheridan, 'Panopticism'
suggested_refs: Surveiller et punir: naissance de la prison (Gallimard, 1975)
sources: Discipline and Punish, trans. Alan Sheridan, foucault.info excerpt

stops.name: Death Valley, LSD at Zabriskie Point
stops.date_confidence: the geography lens dates the trip to May 1975; the day is a placeholder and the account rests on Simeon Wade's memoir, published in 2019
stops.campa: Two young academics, Simeon Wade and Michael Stoneman, drive him out of Claremont into the desert at night with a tape deck and a dose of LSD. They climb to Zabriskie Point and put on Stockhausen and Elisabeth Schwarzkopf while the badlands go on turning colours. Foucault weeps, watches the sky for hours, and says the stars are falling into his skull. He calls it afterwards one of the greatest experiences of his life. He is forty-eight years old and has just published a book about the total administration of bodies.
suggested_refs: Simeon Wade, Foucault in California (2019)

stops.name: San Francisco, the Castro and the baths
stops.date_confidence: the geography lens spans 1975-1983 with no dated visit; July 1975 is a placement inside that span rather than an attested date
stops.campa: Between seminars at Berkeley, which he gives across four separate stays and where he becomes a campus celebrity of a kind France has no equivalent for, he goes into the bathhouses of the Castro and South of Market. He tells friends the place is a laboratory of desire, an invention of pleasures that do not run through the couple, the confession or the doctor, and he means the phrase as a technical one: bodies organizing themselves without a discourse to explain them. Biographers will fight for thirty years over what he caught there and when.
suggested_refs: The bathhouses of San Francisco, 1975-1983, and the Berkeley seminars
sources: James Miller, The Passion of Michel Foucault
Macey, The Lives of Michel Foucault

stops.name: Paris, La Volonte de savoir
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1976 by the chronology lens; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: The first volume of the History of Sexuality is short and hostile to its own century. It argues that the Victorians did not silence sex but made it speak endlessly, in the confessional, the clinic, the school and the census, and that what has been produced by all that talking is not liberation but a science of the individual. He gives power a new shape here: not something held by a sovereign, but something running through health, birth rates and populations, which he names biopower. Five more volumes are announced.
suggested_refs: Histoire de la sexualite I: La Volonte de savoir (Gallimard, 1976)

stops.name: Paris, a rib broken for Klaus Croissant
stops.date_confidence: the chronology lens gives only 1977; the extradition of Klaus Croissant to West Germany takes place in November 1977, so the month and day here are placeholders
stops.campa: The lawyer of the Baader-Meinhof defendants, Klaus Croissant, seeks asylum in France and West Germany asks for him back. Foucault protests the extradition, arguing that a state may not decide which lawyers a defendant is permitted, and is caught in a police charge outside the Sante where Croissant is held. He comes out of it with a fractured rib. He is fifty-one years old and holds a chair at the College de France. The extradition goes ahead in November regardless.
suggested_refs: The Klaus Croissant extradition case, November 1977

stops.name: Tokyo, the lectures on power and madness
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1978 by the chronology lens; the day is a placeholder
stops.campa: On a lecture tour of Japan he speaks in Tokyo on madness, on power, on what he calls an analytic philosophy of politics. Japanese intellectuals ask him whether a history of European reason can be carried out of Europe; he answers that his cannot, and that this is exactly what makes the question worth putting. The talks and interviews of these weeks fill a section of the third volume of the later Dits et ecrits. From Tokyo he goes on into the hills.
suggested_refs: Foucault, Dits et ecrits, vol. III, the 1978 Japan lectures
sources: Foucault, Dits et Ecrits, vol. III

stops.name: Uenohara, zazen at the Seionji temple
stops.date_confidence: the temple is given as Seionji at Uenohara by the chronology lens and as a differently named Rinzai temple by some secondary accounts, with a few placing the retreat near Kyoto; the coordinate is the geocode of Uenohara, Yamanashi, and the identification is a reconstruction
stops.campa: The temple is Rinzai, in the hills of Yamanashi. He sits zazen there for several days with the monk Omori Sogen, in the posture, at the hours, with the stick across his shoulders when he slumps. He asks his hosts continually about the relation between the position of the body and the state of the mind, and they tell him to stop asking. He calls the episode an experiment in techniques of the self. The phrase comes back in the two books he finishes six years later.
suggested_refs: Foucault's 1978 Zen retreat with Omori Sogen; interview on Zen in Dits et ecrits
sources: Foucault, Dits et Ecrits (interview on Zen, 1978)

stops.name: Tehran, reporting the revolution
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1978 by the geography lens; the chronology lens dates the assignment to 1978 after the Black Friday massacre of 8 September
stops.campa: Corriere della Sera sends him to Tehran days after the army fires on the crowd in Jaleh Square. He walks the demonstrations, talks to strikers and mullahs and oil workers, and files dispatches asking what people want when they are willing to die for something a Marxist analysis cannot name. He calls it political spirituality, and says a whole people has decided at once that it prefers death to the Shah. When the revolution produces a state that executes homosexuals, he is attacked for these articles and answers them only briefly.
suggested_refs: Foucault, Iran: chroniques dans Corriere della Sera (1978-1979)

stops.name: Qom, the clerical city
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1978 by the geography lens; the day is a placeholder and the Qom visit shares the dating of the Tehran assignment
stops.campa: He goes down to Qom, the city of the seminaries and the theological schools, and is received by clerics who explain to him what a government founded on religion would be. The historian of the confessional sits on a carpet in a seminary, asking Shia teachers how a faith becomes an instruction to a crowd. He writes that Islam here is not an opiate but the form in which a whole population refuses a modernity imposed on it by a police state with oil money.
suggested_refs: Foucault's Qom interviews, Corriere della Sera, autumn 1978
sources: Foucault, Iran: chroniques dans Corriere della Sera

stops.name: Neauphle-le-Chateau, at the edge of the exile's garden
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the geography lens dates this only to 1978 and tags the contact as disputed among biographers; Khomeini's exile at Neauphle-le-Chateau runs from October 1978, which fixes the month by inference rather than by attestation
stops.campa: Forty kilometres west of Paris, in a rented house behind a hedge in a village of two thousand people, Ruhollah Khomeini receives the world's press under an apple tree and directs a revolution by telephone and cassette tape. Foucault, back from Tehran, comes into this orbit; whether he met the ayatollah, sought a meeting, or only circled the village is disputed by his biographers and not settled by any document in the file. The centre of the Iranian revolution is for four months a garden in the Yvelines.
suggested_refs: Khomeini's residence at Neauphle-le-Chateau, October 1978 to February 1979
sources: Janet Afary and Kevin Anderson, Foucault and the Iranian Revolution (2005)

stops.name: Warsaw, the convoy for Solidarity
stops.date_confidence: the geography lens dates the mission to January 1982, a month after the declaration of martial law; the day is a placeholder and the entry is tagged as a reconstruction in the pool
stops.campa: Jaruzelski declares martial law in December 1981 and the union is outlawed overnight. Foucault joins a convoy carrying medical supplies and printing equipment into Poland for the banned Solidarity, riding in with the doctors and the paper. It is the city where the security services trapped him in 1958 and ended his diplomatic career. He returns to it at fifty-five with a truck. He does not write about it afterwards, and explains it to almost nobody.
suggested_refs: The Medecins du Monde convoy to Poland, January 1982

stops.name: Berkeley, the annual chair he agrees to
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1983 by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: He agrees to teach every year at the University of California at Berkeley, which for a College de France professor amounts to a second country. The seminars he gives there turn on the ancient practice of speaking the truth at one's own risk, and on the care of the self as a discipline rather than a comfort. American students take him for a theorist of power; he tells them, in the plainest sentence he ever gives an interviewer, what he takes himself to be.
stops.quote: I am not a writer, a philosopher, a great figure of intellectual life: I am a teacher.
stops.quote_source: Interview, 'Truth, Power, Self', with Rux Martin, 25 October 1982, in Technologies of the Self (1988)
suggested_refs: The Berkeley seminars of 1983 and the 'Discourse and Truth' lectures
sources: Macey, The Lives of Michel Foucault

stops.name: Paris, 289 rue de Vaugirard, the last two books
stops.date_confidence: the flat is dated 1970s-1984 by the geography lens; January 1984 marks the last College de France course and the final revision of the two volumes, which appear in the spring
stops.campa: In the flat on the rue de Vaugirard, with the books on the walls and Defert in the next room, he finishes the two volumes that abandon the plan announced in 1976: L'Usage des plaisirs and Le Souci de soi, on how Greeks and Romans made an art out of governing themselves before any church required it of them. He gives his last course at the College de France that winter, coughing, to a full hall. The volumes are in the shops in the spring. He is already ill and tells almost nobody.
stops.quote: My role ... is to show people that they are much freer than they feel.
stops.quote_source: Interview, 'Truth, Power, Self', with Rux Martin, 25 October 1982; the ellipsis marks Foucault's own cut, 'and that is too emphatic a word'
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque at 289 rue de Vaugirard, Paris 15e

stops.name: Paris, the Pitie-Salpetriere
stops.date_confidence: attested to 25 June 1984; the pool carries three different coordinates for the hospital and the value used here is the one the afterlife lens settles on
stops.campa: He dies in a neurology ward of the Pitie-Salpetriere at fifty-seven, of an infection secondary to AIDS, the first public figure in France whose death is widely understood to belong to the epidemic, though the hospital bulletin says only a septicaemia. Edmund White reports that he doubted to the end that the disease was real. The building is the old general hospital of the poor of Paris, where Charcot exhibited hysterics to Sigmund Freud in the winter of 1885, and where the confinement of the mad began that he wrote his first book about.
suggested_refs: The Pitie-Salpetriere, Paris 13e; Le Monde obituary coverage, June 1984

stops.name: Vendeuvre-du-Poitou, the village cemetery
stops.date_confidence: attested to 29 June 1984; the pool gives three coordinates for the cemetery, from 0.2833 to 0.3260 in longitude, and the value used here is the midpoint the corrections recommend
stops.campa: He is buried in the cemetery of a village of the Vienne, beside the eighteenth-century family house at 17 route de Poitiers, twenty kilometres from the room in which he was born and in the ground of the medical family whose trade he refused. The ceremony is private, close friends and family, without state honour, without a cathedral, without a minister at the graveside. The most read French philosopher of the century goes into a Poitou churchyard four days after a death whose cause the bulletins would not print.
suggested_refs: The Foucault family plot, Vendeuvre-du-Poitou, Vienne

stops.name: Paris, what Defert does with the death
stops.date_confidence: AIDES is founded in 1984, the month unrecorded in the pool; the later events named here run from 1990 to 2018 and are gathered into this stop rather than given pins of their own
stops.campa: Daniel Defert founds AIDES in the year of the death, partly against the silence and the misinformation that surrounded it, and the charity outlives its occasion by decades. Herve Guibert turns the dying into a novel in 1990 and is attacked for it. The fourteen College de France courses, existing only as tapes and students' notes, are transcribed and published from the 1990s onward and rewrite the scholarship. In 2018 Frederic Gros brings out Les Aveux de la chair, the fourth volume, thirty-four years late.
suggested_refs: AIDES, founded 1984; Les Aveux de la chair (Gallimard, 2018), ed. Frederic Gros
